result.markdown: --- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [export_contract()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-function} | Pointblank description: Export a Pointblank validation or contract to another format. twitter-card: title: >- [export_contract()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-function} | Pointblank description: Export a Pointblank validation or contract to another format. title: >- [export_contract()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-function} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Export a Pointblank validation or contract to another format. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Export a Pointblank validation or contract to another format. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/posit-dev/pointblank/blob/main/pointblank/adapters/_api.py#L267-L428){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature export_contract( validation_or_contract, destination=None, *, format, **kwargs, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Data quality rules written in Pointblank are often useful to tools that don't run Pointblank. An API team may want a JSON Schema, an analytics engineering team may want the tests in a dbt `schema.yml` file, and a data catalog may accept Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS) documents. `export_contract()` translates a [`Contract`](`pointblank.Contract`) or a [`Validate`](`pointblank.Validate`) object into one of these formats, so a single set of rules can be published wherever it's needed. Contracts export most completely because they carry a name, a description, and a [`Schema`](`pointblank.Schema`) with column types. A `Validate` object is exported from the steps in its plan; it doesn't need to be interrogated first. The translation is lossy by nature: only checks that have an equivalent in the target format are written, and the rest are left out without a warning (see the *What Gets Exported* section). To bring a definition back into Pointblank, use [`import_contract()`](`pointblank.import_contract`). ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [validation_or_contract]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The `Contract` or `Validate` object to export. [destination]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : A file path to write the exported document to. Parent directories are created as needed. If `None` (the default), nothing is written and the document is only returned. [format]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The name of the adapter to use: `"json_schema"`, `"frictionless"`, `"dbt"`, or `"odcs"` for the built-in formats, or the name of a custom adapter. This argument is required and must be given by keyword. [**kwargs]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Options for the adapter. None of the built-in adapters currently take any options. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [str | dict]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The exported document. The built-in adapters return it as a dictionary (whether or not it's also written to `destination=`), which can be serialized with `json.dumps()` or `yaml.dump()`. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If no adapter is registered under `format=` (the message lists the available ones), or if the adapter doesn't support exporting. [TypeError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `validation_or_contract` is neither a `Contract` nor a `Validate` object. ::: ## What Gets Exported {.doc-what-gets-exported} The column types come from the contract's schema, and each built-in adapter translates these checks: - **JSON Schema** (`"json_schema"`): a draft 2020-12 object schema whose `title` and `description` come from the contract. `col_vals_not_null()` adds the column to `required`; `col_vals_ge()`/`col_vals_le()` become `minimum`/`maximum`, `col_vals_gt()`/`col_vals_lt()` become `exclusiveMinimum`/`exclusiveMaximum`, and `col_vals_between()` sets both `minimum` and `maximum`. `col_vals_in_set()` becomes `enum`, `col_vals_regex()` becomes `pattern`, `col_vals_eq()` becomes `const`, and `col_vals_within_spec()` becomes a `format` for the `email`, `url`, `ipv4`, and `ipv6` specs. - **Frictionless Table Schema** (`"frictionless"`): a `fields` list with field constraints. `col_vals_not_null()` becomes `required`, `rows_distinct()` becomes `unique`, `col_vals_ge()`/`col_vals_le()` become `minimum`/`maximum`, `col_vals_in_set()` becomes `enum`, and `col_vals_regex()` becomes `pattern`. - **dbt** (`"dbt"`): a `version: 2` document with one model named after the contract. `col_vals_not_null()`, `rows_distinct()`, and `col_vals_in_set()` become the generic tests `not_null`, `unique`, and `accepted_values`. - **Open Data Contract Standard** (`"odcs"`): a `DataContract` document with an `info` block and one dataset table. `col_vals_not_null()` sets `isNullable: false`, `rows_distinct()` sets `isUnique`, `col_vals_in_set()` becomes `enum`, `col_vals_regex()` becomes `pattern`, and `col_vals_ge()`/`col_vals_le()` become `minimum`/`maximum`. Any other step, along with thresholds, actions, and owner information, isn't exported. When `destination=` is given, the JSON Schema and Frictionless documents are written as JSON and the dbt document as YAML. ODCS documents are written as JSON if the path ends in `.json` and as YAML otherwise. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Let's start with a `Contract` for a table of orders. It has a schema with column types, a description, and a mix of checks. ::: {#9b31ac41 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pointblank as pb import json orders_contract = pb.Contract( name="orders", description="One row per customer order.", schema=pb.Schema(order_id="Int64", status="String", amount="Float64"), steps=[ pb.Step("col_vals_not_null", columns=["order_id", "status"]), pb.Step("rows_distinct", columns_subset="order_id"), pb.Step("col_vals_in_set", columns="status", set=["placed", "shipped", "returned"]), pb.Step("col_vals_between", columns="amount", left=0, right=10000), ], ) ``` ::: Exporting it as a JSON Schema gives us a dictionary, which we can print with `json.dumps()`. ::: {#e8dd77e0 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} orders_json_schema = pb.export_contract(orders_contract, format="json_schema") print(json.dumps(orders_json_schema, indent=2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` { "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema", "type": "object", "title": "orders", "description": "One row per customer order.", "properties": { "order_id": { "type": "integer" }, "status": { "type": "string", "enum": [ "placed", "shipped", "returned" ] }, "amount": { "type": "number", "minimum": 0, "maximum": 10000 } }, "required": [ "order_id", "status" ] } ``` ::: ::: The Pointblank types became JSON types, the not-null check filled the `required` list, the set of statuses became an `enum`, and the range check became `minimum` and `maximum` values. The `rows_distinct()` step was left out because JSON Schema has no way to say that a value must be unique across records. The same contract can be written out as a dbt `schema.yml` file. Here we write it to a `models` directory (which is created if it doesn't exist) and print the file's contents. ::: {#9a2e0c5b .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} from pathlib import Path pb.export_contract(orders_contract, "models/schema.yml", format="dbt") print(Path("models/schema.yml").read_text()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` version: 2 models: - name: orders description: One row per customer order. columns: - name: order_id data_type: integer data_tests: - not_null - unique - name: status data_type: string data_tests: - not_null - accepted_values: values: - placed - shipped - returned - name: amount data_type: float data_tests: [] ``` ::: ::: This time the uniqueness check is kept (as dbt's `unique` test) but the range check is not, since dbt has no generic test for it. The `amount` column is still listed, with its type and an empty list of tests. An exported document can be imported again with `import_contract()`. Doing so is a quick way to see which rules survive the round trip. ::: {#5885050c .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(pb.import_contract(orders_json_schema).summary()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Contract Import Summary Format: json_schema Format version: https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema Columns detected: 3 Constraints mapped: 5 Coverage: 100% ``` ::: ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~import_contract`) : Import an external definition into Pointblank. [](`~list_adapters`) : List the formats available for import and export. [](`~register_adapter`) : Add support for another format. [](`~Contract`) : The declarative contract that exports most completely.
